Pallor is unusual paleness of the skin and/or mucous membranes, and is a sign of anaemia.

Palmar pallor: hold the child's palm open by grasping it gently from the side. Do not stretch the fingers backwards (this may cause pallor by blocking the blood supply). Compare the colour of the child's palm with your own palm and with the palms of other children. The child has some palmar pallor if the skin of the child's palm is pale. The child has severe palmar pallor if the skin of the palm is very pale or so pale that it looks white.

Conjunctival pallor: pull the lower eyelid gently down and look at the palpebral conjunctiva if the conjunctiva is abnormally pale (moderate pallor) or even white (severe pallor).

Sunken eyes: the eyes of a dehydrated child may appear sunken. Check whether the eyes are sunken. Then ask the mother if she thinks that there is something different in the eyes of her child. Her opinion helps you determine if the eyes are sunken. Note: in severely malnourished children who are visibly wasted (who have marasmus), the eyes always look sunken even if the child is not dehydrated. Even though sunken eyes is a less reliable sign in a visibly wasted child, it should nevertheless still be used in classifying the dehydration status of the child.

Lethargic: a child is lethargic when not reacting to what is happening- possibly staring into space.

Unconscious: a child is unconscious when not reacting to different stimuli/stimulations.

Skin pinch: put the child on the examination table, back elongated, arms by the side of the body (not above the head) and the arms straight. Or ask the mother to hold the child flat on her lap. Choose a location from the abdomen between the umbilicus and the side of the abdomen, and pinch the skin with your thumb and index finger. Place the hand so that the fold goes in the direction of the length of the child's body and not across the body. It is important to firmly grasp all layers of skin and subcutaneous tissue for one second then release them. Observe if the skin fold disappears: very slowly, over more than 2 seconds; slowly, the fold remains marked even for a brief moment; immediately. Note: in children with severe malnutrition (marasmus) the skin fold may disappear slowly even if the child is not dehydrated. In children who are overweight or have oedema the fold may fade immediately even if the child is dehydrated. Although the skinfold test is less reliable in these children, it must be used to classify their dehydration.

Convulsions are:
  • Repetitive movements of the limbs (one or all 4) which cannot be stopped by touching
  • Or repetitive movements of the face such as chewing, blinking of the eyes, ocular deviation, rictus of the corner of the mouth, grimaces
  • Or a generalised rigidity for more than 30 seconds
Convulsions are generally associated with:
  • A change in consciousness, eyes open with a fixed or deviated gaze (absent)
  • A change in the rhythm of breathing
  • A post-critical phase of sleep or fatigue after convulsion
NOTE: Do not confuse with the shiver of a child with a rapidly rising temperature, movements of fine tremors that can be stopped to the touch.

Pinçamento da pele: coloque a criança na mesa de exame com as costas alongadas e os braços não dobrados ao lado do corpo (não acima da cabeça). Ou então peça à mãe para segurar a criança deitada em seu colo. Escolha um local no abdômen entre o umbigo e a lateral do abdômen e pince a pele com o polegar e o indicador. A dobra deve ser na direção do comprimento do corpo da criança, e não na transversal. É importante pinçar firmemente todas as camadas da pele e o tecido subcutâneo por um segundo e depois soltar. Observe se a prega cutânea desaparece: muito lentamente (leva mais de 2 segundos); lentamente (a prega permanece visível, mesmo que por um instante); imediatamente. Observação: em crianças com desnutrição grave (marasmo), a prega cutânea pode desaparecer lentamente, mesmo que a criança não esteja desidratada. Em crianças com excesso de peso ou com edema, a dobra pode desaparecer imediatamente, mesmo que a criança esteja desidratada. Embora o teste de prega cutânea seja menos confiável nessas crianças, deve ser usado para classificar a desidratação delas.

As convulsões são:
  • Movimentos repetitivos dos membros (um ou todos os 4) que não podem ser interrompidos tocando-os
  • Ou movimentos repetitivos do rosto, como mastigação, piscar dos olhos, desvio ocular, contração do canto da boca, caretas
  • Ou uma rigidez generalizada por mais de 30 segundos
As convulsões são geralmente associadas a:
  • Alteração da consciência, olhos abertos com olhar fixo ou desviado (ausente)
  • Alteração do ritmo respiratório
  • Uma fase pós-crítica de sono ou fadiga depois da convulsão
